label: Wheals and episodic swelling
q: Is this ordinary urticaria, vasculitis, or bradykinin-mediated angioedema?
lead: The whole differential turns on one question that costs nothing to ask: how long does an individual wheal last? Under 24 hours means urticaria. Over 24 hours, with bruising, burning or arthralgia, means vasculitis and needs a biopsy. Swelling without wheals, unresponsive to antihistamines, means bradykinin — and adrenaline will not work on it.

stop.l: Stridor, hoarseness, or swelling of the tongue or pharynx
stop.a: Airway. Intramuscular adrenaline, call for anesthetic help, and prepare for a surgical airway. Treat as anaphylaxis until it declares otherwise.

stop.l: Wheeze, hypotension, or gastrointestinal cramping with the eruption
stop.a: Anaphylaxis. Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh, repeated at 5 minutes. Antihistamines are adjunctive and never first.

stop.l: Angioedema on an ACE inhibitor, no urticaria, no response to adrenaline
stop.a: Bradykinin-mediated. Stop the ACE inhibitor permanently and switch class — not to an ARB in the first instance. Consider icatibant or C1-inhibitor concentrate. Adrenaline, steroids and antihistamines will not reverse it, and relying on them is what leads to airway loss.

stop.l: Recurrent facial or laryngeal swelling with abdominal crises and a family history
stop.a: Hereditary angioedema. Check C4, C1-esterase inhibitor level and function. Attacks are treated with C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant.

stop.l: Fever, arthralgia and wheals lasting more than 24 hours
stop.a: Urticarial vasculitis or a systemic autoinflammatory syndrome. Biopsy, complement levels, ESR, and urinalysis for red cell casts.

stop.l: Widespread flushing with syncope after minor rubbing of lesions
stop.a: Consider systemic mastocytosis. Serum tryptase. Avoid opiates, NSAIDs and radiocontrast until assessed.

stop.l: Urticarial eruption in the third trimester that begins around the umbilicus or blisters
stop.a: Pemphigoid gestationis, not polymorphic eruption of pregnancy. Perilesional direct immunofluorescence and BP180 ELISA, with obstetric referral and fetal surveillance - there is a risk of prematurity and small-for-gestational-age birth, and the newborn can blister.

dx.look: Urticarial or annular polycyclic plaques, often with dusky centers, accompanied by fever and arthralgia, appearing 1 to 3 weeks after a drug (classically cefaclor) or infection, mostly in children; unlike true serum sickness there is no immune-complex vasculitis or renal disease.
fr: Urticarial or annular plaques with fever and joint pain
Onset 1 to 3 weeks after a drug (cefaclor, other antibiotics) or infection
Children more than adults
Facial or acral edema
Self-limited over 1 to 2 weeks after stopping the drug
ag: Individual wheals persisting beyond 24 hours with bruising
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis - stop the suspected drug and it resolves over 1 to 2 weeks; distinguish urticarial vasculitis (biopsy if wheals last over 24 hours and bruise).
dx.hp: If biopsied, a sparse perivascular infiltrate with dermal edema and no true vasculitis.
dx.assoc: A type III-like hypersensitivity to a drug (classically cefaclor) or infection; unlike true serum sickness there is no hypocomplementemia, immune-complex vasculitis or nephritis.
dx.mgmt: Stop the culprit drug; antihistamines and a short corticosteroid course control symptoms. Document the drug as an allergy and avoid re-exposure.

dx.look: Sharply defined wheals, from under 1 cm to over 8 cm, erythematous or white with an erythematous rim, round, annular or serpiginous, migrating over hours. Individual lesions resolve within 24 hours leaving normal skin. Often with angioedema. Lasts under 6 weeks.
fr: Individual wheals resolve within 24 hours
Lesions migrate — new sites appear as old ones fade
Skin returns to normal with no bruising or scale
Clear trigger: food, drug, infection, insect sting
Duration under 6 weeks
ag: A single wheal persisting beyond 24 hours
Residual purpura or pigmentation at resolved sites
dx.cf: Clinical. No investigation is needed in uncomplicated acute urticaria with an evident trigger. Resist the temptation to send a screen.
dx.hp: Biopsy is not part of the diagnosis and should be reserved for wheals that outlast 24 hours. A specimen would show papillary dermal edema with dilated venules and lymphatics and a sparse perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils and neutrophils, with intact vessel walls and no leukocytoclasis.
dx.assoc: Often postviral or drug/food-related; individual wheals last under 24 hours and clear without bruising. Angioedema may accompany it - watch for airway or systemic features.
dx.mgmt: A second-generation H1-antihistamine (up-dosed as needed); a short oral corticosteroid course for severe flares; epinephrine if anaphylaxis.

dx.look: Daily or near-daily wheals for more than 6 weeks, with no identifiable external trigger in about 80%. Up to 40% have functional autoantibodies against FcεRI or IgE. Twice as common in women. Roughly 40% still have it a decade later.
fr: Present most days for more than 6 weeks
No consistent identifiable trigger
Individual wheals still resolve within 24 hours
Responds, at least partially, to antihistamines
Associated autoimmune thyroid disease
dx.cf: FBC, ESR or CRP, and thyroid function with anti-thyroid antibodies is a reasonable minimum. Autologous serum skin test for autoimmune urticaria where available. A broad allergy screen has almost no yield here and creates false leads.
dx.hp: Sparse perivascular lymphocytes and dermal edema; a neutrophil-rich or vessel-damaging pattern should redirect toward urticarial vasculitis.
dx.assoc: Mostly autoimmune; a minimal work-up (CBC, ESR or CRP, thyroid function and antibodies) suffices - broad allergy panels have low yield. Look for thyroid autoimmunity.
dx.mgmt: A second-generation antihistamine up-titrated to fourfold; add omalizumab, then cyclosporine, for antihistamine-refractory disease.

dx.look: Wheals reproducibly provoked by a defined physical stimulus: stroking (dermographism, in about 4% of the population), cold, pressure, vibration, water, sunlight, or a rise in core temperature (cholinergic, giving tiny 2–3 mm papular wheals on a wide flare).
fr: Reproducible with a specific physical stimulus
Confined to the site of the stimulus
Dermographism: linear wheals along scratch lines within minutes
Cholinergic: pinpoint wheals with exercise, heat or emotion
Cold: wheals on rewarming after cold exposure
ag: Random distribution with no relation to any stimulus
dx.cf: Provocation testing confirms it and is quick: stroke the skin for dermographism, an ice cube for cold urticaria, exercise or a warm bath for cholinergic, and calibrated UV for solar urticaria. In cold urticaria, warn about swimming — whole-body cold immersion has caused fatalities.
dx.hp: Biopsy adds nothing - provocation with the suspected stimulus is the diagnostic step. A wheal raised by the trigger shows the same dermal edema and sparse perivascular infiltrate as any urticaria, with no vessel-wall damage to explain a physical cause.
dx.assoc: Reproduced by the relevant trigger (dermographism, cold, cholinergic, pressure, solar); cold urticaria carries an anaphylaxis risk with aquatic immersion.
dx.mgmt: Trigger avoidance plus a second-generation antihistamine; carry epinephrine for cold urticaria with systemic reactions.

dx.look: Wheals that last more than 24 hours, burn or hurt rather than itch, and resolve leaving purpura or hyperpigmentation. Arthralgia, fever and raised ESR are usual. Hypocomplementemic disease is associated with lupus, Sjögren syndrome and chronic obstructive lung disease.
fr: Individual lesion persists beyond 24 hours
Burning or pain rather than itch
Residual bruising or brown staining
Arthralgia, fever, raised ESR
Low C3, C4 or C1q
dx.cf: Biopsy a lesion that has been present for less than 48 hours. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of postcapillary venules confirms it. Then complement levels, ANA, ENA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis serology and urinalysis for red cell casts.
dx.hp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis - neutrophils, nuclear dust and fibrinoid vessel-wall change; direct immunofluorescence may show immune deposits.
dx.assoc: Wheals lasting over 24 hours with burning and bruising; check complement - hypocomplementemic disease links to SLE and anti-C1q. Screen for connective-tissue disease.
dx.mgmt: Treat the cause; NSAIDs, colchicine, dapsone or hydroxychloroquine for skin-limited disease; systemic immunosuppression for hypocomplementemic or systemic disease.

dx.look: Deep, non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling of face, lips, tongue, larynx, extremities or bowel wall, without wheals. Develops over hours and resolves over 2–5 days. Does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamine or corticosteroid. Hereditary form gives recurrent abdominal crises presenting as a surgical abdomen.
fr: Swelling without any wheals
No itch
Failure to respond to adrenaline and antihistamines
On an ACE inhibitor, at any point in the course of treatment
Family history with abdominal pain attacks
Attacks provoked by trauma, dental work or stress
dx.cf: C4 is the screening test — it is low during and usually between attacks in hereditary angioedema. Then C1-esterase inhibitor antigenic level and functional assay. ACE inhibitor angioedema is a clinical diagnosis with normal complement, and can begin years into treatment.
dx.hp: Biopsy is not performed - C4 with C1-esterase inhibitor level and function is the test that separates this from mast cell driven swelling. A specimen would show deep dermal and subcutaneous edema with dilated lymphatics and very few inflammatory cells, without the eosinophils and mast cell degranulation of histaminergic angioedema.
dx.assoc: No wheals and unresponsive to antihistamines or epinephrine; think ACE-inhibitor-induced, or hereditary or acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency - check C4 (low), and C1-inhibitor level and function.
dx.mgmt: Stop any ACE inhibitor; for C1-inhibitor disease use C1-inhibitor concentrate, icatibant or ecallantide acutely with specific prophylaxis - not antihistamines or steroids.

dx.look: Fixed red-brown macules and papules, most often on the trunk, which urticate when rubbed — the Darier sign. Flushing, headache, diarrhea and, in systemic disease, syncope. In children it usually resolves; in adults it usually persists.
fr: Fixed brown macules that are always in the same place
Darier sign: rubbing produces a palpable wheal within 5–10 minutes
Flushing, diarrhea, headache
Onset in early childhood
ag: Migrating wheals with no fixed pigmented lesion
dx.cf: Elicit the Darier sign at the bedside with the blunt end of a pen — wait up to 10 minutes. Biopsy with Giemsa or tryptase immunostain. Serum tryptase above 20 ng/mL suggests systemic involvement and warrants hematology referral.
dx.dsc: Light-brown reticular or blotchy pigmentation; stroking a lesion produces urtication (the Darier sign).
dx.hp: Increased dermal mast cells (highlighted by CD117, tryptase or Giemsa) around vessels and in the papillary dermis.
dx.assoc: The Darier sign is characteristic; check serum tryptase and, in adults, consider KIT D816V and systemic disease. Avoid mast-cell degranulators (opioids, NSAIDs, radiocontrast, alcohol).
dx.mgmt: Trigger avoidance with H1 and H2 antihistamines; oral cromolyn for GI symptoms; carry epinephrine if anaphylaxis. Childhood disease often resolves by puberty.

dx.look: An elderly patient with persistent, intensely itchy urticarial plaques that do not migrate as true wheals do, present for weeks to months, with no blisters yet. Regularly treated as chronic urticaria for a long time before the first bulla appears.
fr: Age over 65
Fixed rather than migrating plaques
Present for weeks with severe itch
Poor response to antihistamines
Peripheral eosinophilia
dx.cf: Perilesional direct immunofluorescence and BP180 ELISA. Consider this diagnosis in any elderly patient with itchy urticarial plaques that have failed antihistamines — catching it before blistering changes the whole course.
dx.hp: A subepidermal blister with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane, and on salt-split skin the deposits sit on the blister roof.
dx.assoc: Elderly patients; associated with neurologic disease (dementia, stroke, Parkinson) and occasionally drugs (gliptins, PD-1 inhibitors); a pre-bullous urticarial phase is common. Serum BP180/BP230 ELISA supports the diagnosis.
dx.mgmt: A potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol) is first-line and as effective as oral steroids for many; systemic prednisone with a steroid-sparing agent (doxycycline, methotrexate, azathioprine) for extensive disease.
dx.pat: Lower trunk, flexures and inner thighs

dx.look: Crops of firm, intensely itchy 3 to 10 mm urticarial papules, many with a central punctum, on exposed skin - forearms, lower legs, ankles and the waistband line. Individual lesions last days rather than hours, are excoriated, and blister readily in young children. New crops appear as old ones fade and leave hyperpigmented marks.
fr: Firm papules with a central punctum on exposed skin
The individual lesion persists for several days
Grouped or linear clusters of three (breakfast, lunch and dinner)
Children, travelers, a new pet, or a seasonal pattern
Bullous lesions in a young child
Covered skin is spared
ag: True wheals migrating and clearing within hours
Complete clearance on an antihistamine alone
dx.cf: Clinical. The work is in the exposure history - pets, bedding, soft furnishings, travel, outdoor work - and in inspecting the environment. Lesions stop appearing once the source is eradicated, which is both the treatment and the confirmation.
dx.hp: A wedge-shaped superficial and deep perivascular infiltrate with eosinophils and marked dermal edema; a bite reaction pattern rather than true urticaria.
dx.assoc: Delayed hypersensitivity to arthropod saliva - fleas, bed bugs, mosquitoes, mites. Household members are often unaffected because sensitization differs. Heavily excoriated persistent papules in an adult should prompt an HIV test, since papular pruritic eruption of HIV is the same reaction pattern in advanced disease.
dx.mgmt: Eradicate the source - treat pets and the home, launder and heat-treat bedding, use permethrin-treated clothing and DEET. A mid-potency topical corticosteroid and a sedating antihistamine at night for symptoms; antibiotics only for genuine secondary infection.

dx.look: Itch, burning and wheals appearing within 15 to 30 minutes at the exact point of contact, settling within an hour or two once the substance is removed. The immunologic form (latex, raw fish, meat, flour, animal dander) can generalize and progress to anaphylaxis. The nonimmunologic form (sorbic acid, benzoic acid, cinnamic aldehyde, nettle) stays local and occurs in anyone.
fr: Wheals within 15 to 30 minutes of contact, at the contact site
Clears within 1 to 2 hours once the contact is removed
Reproducible every single time the substance is handled
Occupational pattern that clears on days off and on vacation
Latex gloves, raw food handling, hairdressing or health care work
Burning and stinging rather than pure itch
ag: Random distribution unrelated to any contact
dx.cf: Open application test on intact skin, read at 20, 40 and 60 minutes, working from the least to the most invasive method. Skin prick testing and specific IgE for latex and food proteins. Test where resuscitation facilities are available, because the immunologic form can generalize.
dx.hp: Dermal edema with a sparse perivascular infiltrate; biopsy is not needed and cannot separate the immunologic from the nonimmunologic form.
dx.assoc: Latex allergy cross-reacts with banana, avocado, kiwi and chestnut and carries a real risk of intraoperative anaphylaxis - flag it prominently in the record. Protein contact dermatitis in food handlers presents as chronic hand eczema that flares within minutes of handling the food, and is missed because patch tests are negative.
dx.mgmt: Avoidance, with nonlatex gloves and barrier measures at work, and occupational health involvement. An oral antihistamine before unavoidable exposure; an epinephrine autoinjector and allergy referral for anyone who has had systemic features.

dx.look: Severe itch with 1 to 3 mm erythematous papules that coalesce into polycyclic urticarial plaques with blanched halos, beginning inside the abdominal striae distensae and spreading to buttocks, thighs, upper inner arms and lower back. Periumbilical skin is characteristically spared. Onset averages 36 weeks in a first pregnancy, and it clears within 1 to 2 weeks of delivery.
fr: Third trimester, first pregnancy, or a multiple pregnancy
Lesions begin within the abdominal striae distensae
Periumbilical sparing
Buttocks, thighs and upper inner arms involved
Severe itch with surprisingly few excoriations
Face, palms and soles spared
ag: Recurrence in every subsequent pregnancy, earlier each time
dx.cf: Clinical. The one diagnosis to exclude is pemphigoid gestationis, which starts periumbilically, blisters, and carries fetal risk - perilesional direct immunofluorescence and BP180 ELISA settle it. Routine bloods and histology are noncontributory in polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.
dx.hp: A nonspecific superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal edema and variable spongiosis; direct immunofluorescence is negative, which is the reason for doing it.
dx.assoc: No fetal or maternal risk. Associated with first pregnancy, multiple pregnancy and greater maternal weight gain. Recurrence in a later pregnancy is uncommon and milder when it happens, and it does not recur with oral contraceptives.
dx.mgmt: A potent topical corticosteroid with emollients, tapered as it settles. Oral prednisone 10 to 40 mg daily relieves severe itch within 24 hours and is safe in the third trimester. Oral antihistamines are largely ineffective here.

dx.n: NSAID and pseudoallergen-induced urticaria and angioedema
dx.look: Wheals, facial and periorbital angioedema, or both, appearing 20 minutes to 4 hours after aspirin, an NSAID, an opioid or radiocontrast. It is not IgE-mediated: it occurs on a first exposure, is dose-related, and cross-reacts across all COX-1 inhibitors regardless of chemical class. Established chronic urticaria flares rather than starts.
fr: Onset 20 minutes to 4 hours after the drug
Reaction on a first-ever exposure, with no sensitizing course
Cross-reaction to chemically unrelated NSAIDs
Facial and periorbital angioedema prominent
Asthma with nasal polyps and chronic rhinosinusitis
Underlying chronic urticaria that flares with any NSAID
ag: Reaction to one drug with proven tolerance of other NSAIDs
Onset days into a course rather than within hours
Positive specific IgE to the drug
dx.cf: The history is the diagnosis. Skin tests and specific IgE are negative and unhelpful because the mechanism is not IgE-mediated. A supervised graded oral challenge establishes a safe alternative analgesic, which is the part that changes daily life.
dx.hp: Dermal edema with a sparse perivascular infiltrate, indistinguishable from other urticaria.
dx.assoc: COX-1 inhibition shunting arachidonic acid toward cysteinyl leukotrienes. Screen for aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease - asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Radiocontrast reactions recur in 25 to 35% of those with a prior reaction, so premedicate or use an alternative agent.
dx.mgmt: Avoid all COX-1 inhibitors and document the whole class, not the single drug, as the problem. Antihistamines for the acute event, epinephrine if there are systemic features. Then establish a tolerated alternative by supervised challenge rather than leaving someone with no analgesic at all.
dx.pat: Facial and periorbital angioedema with wheals

dx.look: Generalized wheals and flushing within minutes to 2 hours of an allergen, together with at least one of airway compromise, hypotension, or persistent gastrointestinal symptoms. The warning signs that precede collapse are itching of the palms, soles and scalp, sudden fatigue, yawning, a metallic taste, sneezing and a sense of impending doom.
fr: Wheals with wheeze, stridor, hypotension or collapse
Onset within minutes to 2 hours of a food, sting, drug or latex
Vomiting, crampy abdominal pain or diarrhea with the eruption
Itching of the palms, soles and scalp at onset
Rapid improvement after intramuscular epinephrine
ag: Skin findings alone with normal vital signs
Swelling with no wheals that does not respond to epinephrine
dx.cf: Clinical, and treatment must not wait for any test. Serum tryptase at 1 to 2 hours and again at 24 hours supports it retrospectively - a rise then fall confirms mast cell activation. Refer for allergen-specific IgE and skin prick testing 4 to 6 weeks later, once mediator stores have recovered.
dx.hp: Not applicable - the diagnosis is clinical and biopsy has no role in the acute event.
dx.assoc: Food (peanut, tree nut, shellfish), hymenoptera venom, beta-lactams, latex, and food-dependent exercise-induced reactions. A baseline tryptase above 20 ng/mL after recovery points to clonal mast cell disease. Beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors worsen the reaction and blunt the response to epinephrine.
dx.mgmt: Intramuscular epinephrine 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh, repeated at 5 minutes, with supine positioning and legs raised, oxygen and fluids. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjunctive and never first. Observe 6 to 12 hours for a biphasic reaction, then discharge with two epinephrine autoinjectors, a written plan and an allergy referral.

dx.n: Autoinflammatory urticarial syndrome (cryopyrinopathy or Schnitzler syndrome)
dx.look: Recurrent urticarial papules and plaques that itch little or burn, accompanied by fever, arthralgia, conjunctivitis, bone pain and a persistently raised CRP. Individual lesions may outlast 24 hours but leave no purpura and no bruising. Cryopyrinopathies begin in infancy and are autosomal dominant; Schnitzler syndrome begins after 40 with a monoclonal IgM.
fr: Wheals with quotidian or periodic fever over months to years
Bone pain, arthralgia and conjunctivitis
CRP, ESR and serum amyloid A raised even between attacks
Onset in infancy with a dominant family history
Onset after age 40 with a monoclonal IgM paraprotein
Progressive sensorineural hearing loss
ag: A clear external trigger for every episode
dx.cf: CRP, ESR and serum amyloid A, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation for a monoclonal IgM, and a lesional biopsy showing neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis. NLRP3 sequencing confirms a cryopyrinopathy, but somatic mosaicism means a negative result does not exclude it.
dx.hp: Neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis - dermal edema with perivascular and perieccrine neutrophils and leukocytoclasia, without fibrinoid vessel-wall necrosis.
dx.assoc: Untreated disease progresses to sensorineural deafness, vision loss and AA amyloidosis with renal failure, which is the reason the diagnosis matters. Schnitzler syndrome carries a risk of evolution to Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, so the paraprotein needs monitoring.
dx.mgmt: Refer to rheumatology or clinical immunology. Interleukin-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) is dramatically effective and works almost as a therapeutic test. Antihistamines do not control it and corticosteroids only partly do.

ctx.s: The 6-week line defines chronic urticaria, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

ctx.l: On an ACE inhibitor or ARB
ctx.s: ACE inhibitor angioedema can begin years into therapy, Fitzpatrick 8e §14
Hereditary angioedema is autosomal dominant, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

ctx.l: Known autoimmune or connective tissue disease
ctx.s: Urticarial vasculitis accompanies SLE and Sjögren syndrome, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

ctx.l: Recent infection, new drug, or food exposure
Currently pregnant, in the third trimester or just delivered
ctx.s: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy peaks at 36 weeks, Fitzpatrick 8e §15

ctx.l: Outdoor exposure, travel, a new pet, or a household with fleas or bed bugs

find.l: Individual wheal resolves within 24 hours
find.s: The 24-hour rule is the single most discriminating question in this presentation, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Lesions leave bruising or brown staining
Burning or pain rather than itch
Arthralgia, fever or raised ESR
Deep swelling with no wheals at all
No response to antihistamine, steroid or adrenaline
find.s: Bradykinin-mediated swelling is refractory to mast cell directed therapy, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Reproducible with a defined physical stimulus
Linear wheals appear along scratch lines within minutes
Pinpoint 2–3 mm wheals on a wide flare after exercise or heat
Fixed brown macules that urticate when rubbed (Darier sign)
Plaques are fixed in place rather than migrating
Peripheral eosinophilia
Abdominal pain attacks, sometimes mistaken for a surgical abdomen
find.s: Bowel wall angioedema in hereditary angioedema, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Flushing, diarrhea or headache accompanying the skin lesions
Urticarial plaques with fever and arthralgia 1 to 3 weeks after a drug
Grouped or linear excoriated papules with a central punctum on exposed skin
find.s: Papular urticaria from arthropod bites, Fitzpatrick 8e §28

find.l: Only uncovered skin is affected, with a seasonal, travel or new-pet history
Wheals appear within 30 minutes at the exact site of contact and clear within 2 hours
Itch and swelling on donning latex gloves or handling raw food, easing away from work
find.s: Immunologic contact urticaria to latex and food proteins, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Pregnant in the third trimester with itchy papules starting inside abdominal striae
Periumbilical skin spared, with lesions on thighs, buttocks and upper inner arms
find.s: Periumbilical sparing separates polymorphic eruption of pregnancy from pemphigoid gestationis, Fitzpatrick 8e §15, §6

find.l: Wheals or swelling 20 minutes to 4 hours after aspirin, an NSAID or an opioid
Asthma with nasal polyps, or a reaction to more than one chemically unrelated NSAID
find.s: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, Andrews' Diseases of the Skin

find.l: Wheeze, stridor, hypotension or collapse within 2 hours of an exposure
Flushing, throat tightness, palmar itch and a sense of impending doom with the wheals
find.s: Premonitory symptoms of IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Wheals with recurrent fever and bone pain over months to years
Sensorineural hearing loss, conjunctivitis, or a monoclonal IgM paraprotein
Annular polycyclic urticarial plaques with dusky centers, with swelling of the hands and feet
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - dusky annular plaques with acral edema in serum sickness-like reaction

test.w: Any wheal that has been present in one place for more than 24 hours, that burns rather than itches, or that leaves purpura behind.
test.p: Fibrinoid necrosis of postcapillary venules with a neutrophilic infiltrate and nuclear dust confirms urticarial vasculitis. Then look for the systemic association.
test.n: A negative biopsy from a lesion under 24 hours old is uninterpretable, and from a lesion over 48 hours old is unreliable. The window matters.
test.x: Circle the lesion with a pen and ask the patient to return when they can confirm it has been there for 24 hours. This one step converts a guess into a diagnosis.

test.l: C4, C1-esterase inhibitor level and functional assay
test.w: Angioedema without wheals, especially when recurrent, familial, associated with abdominal pain, or unresponsive to adrenaline.
test.p: Low C4 with reduced C1-inhibitor level (type 1, 85%) or normal level with reduced function (type 2, 15%) confirms hereditary angioedema. Refer for on-demand and prophylactic therapy and family screening.
test.n: Normal complement with ACE inhibitor exposure indicates drug-induced bradykinin angioedema. Stop the drug permanently.
test.x: C4 is the practical screening test because it stays low between attacks. Acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency, which is associated with lymphoproliferative disease, additionally shows a low C1q — request it in new-onset disease after age 40.

test.w: Fixed pigmented lesions with a positive Darier sign, unexplained flushing with syncope, or anaphylaxis without an identified allergen.
test.p: A baseline above 20 ng/mL suggests systemic mastocytosis. Refer to hematology for marrow assessment and KIT D816V testing.
test.n: A normal baseline tryptase does not exclude cutaneous mastocytosis, which is often confined to the skin.
test.x: A level drawn during an acute reaction reflects degranulation, not baseline burden. Draw the baseline at least 24 hours after any acute event.

test.l: Provocation testing for the suspected physical trigger
test.w: Whenever the history suggests a reproducible physical stimulus. It takes minutes and converts a vague chronic urticaria label into a specific, manageable diagnosis.
test.p: A wheal at the site of the applied stimulus confirms the subtype and directs both avoidance advice and dosing.
test.n: A negative test does not exclude an inducible urticaria that is currently suppressed by antihistamines. Repeat after 3 days off treatment.
test.x: Cold urticaria carries a genuine risk of systemic reaction with whole-body cold exposure. Confirm it, then counsel explicitly against swimming in cold water — that conversation is the point of making the diagnosis.

test.l: Perilesional direct immunofluorescence and BP180 ELISA
test.w: An elderly patient with persistent itchy urticarial plaques that have failed adequate antihistamine therapy, even with no blisters.
test.p: Linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone confirms pemphigoid in its pre-bullous phase. Treating now, before blistering, changes the course.
test.n: Negative direct IF from correctly sampled perilesional skin argues strongly against it.
test.x: This diagnosis is routinely delayed by months because the pre-bullous phase is labeled chronic urticaria. Age over 65 with fixed itchy plaques should trigger the biopsy.

test.l: FBC, ESR or CRP, thyroid function with anti-thyroid antibodies
test.w: Chronic spontaneous urticaria, as a limited baseline screen. This is the whole appropriate workup in the absence of systemic features.
test.p: A raised ESR points away from simple chronic urticaria and toward vasculitis or a systemic cause. Thyroid autoimmunity is a common association.
test.n: Normal results support ordinary chronic spontaneous urticaria and are worth showing the patient — reassurance is part of the treatment.
test.x: Extensive allergy panels and food-specific IgE testing have almost no diagnostic yield in chronic spontaneous urticaria and generate false leads that lead to unnecessary dietary restriction.

test.l: Serum tryptase at 1 to 2 hours and repeated at 24 hours
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §23; accuracy figures are a calibrated estimate
test.w: After any urticarial event with airway, circulatory or gastrointestinal involvement. Draw it during treatment - it must not delay epinephrine.
test.p: A rise at 1 to 2 hours that falls by 24 hours confirms mast cell degranulation and settles the argument about whether the event was truly anaphylaxis.
test.n: A normal acute tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis, particularly food-triggered reactions, where it is often normal. The diagnosis stays clinical.
test.x: The single sample is nearly useless without the paired baseline. If the 24-hour value is also above 20 ng/mL, the problem is a clonal mast cell disorder, not a one-off allergy.

test.l: Open application test, then skin prick testing and specific IgE to latex
test.w: Any wheal that appears at a contact site within an hour, and any occupational hand eruption that flares within minutes of handling food or wearing gloves.
test.p: A wheal at the application site within 20 to 60 minutes confirms contact urticaria. Positive latex IgE means flagging the record for surgery and dentistry, and counseling about banana, avocado, kiwi and chestnut.
test.n: A negative open test on intact skin does not exclude it - repeat on slightly abraded or previously affected skin, which is where the immunologic form is most reactive.
test.x: Start with the open test, not the prick test, and have resuscitation facilities present. Immunologic contact urticaria to latex or food protein can generalize into anaphylaxis during testing.

test.l: Supervised graded oral challenge with an alternative analgesic
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin; accuracy figures are a calibrated estimate
test.w: After a convincing history of urticaria or angioedema within hours of aspirin or an NSAID, when an analgesic or antiplatelet agent is still needed.
test.p: A reaction during challenge confirms the mechanism and defines the whole COX-1 class as unsafe, not just the index drug.
test.n: Tolerance of acetaminophen or a selective COX-2 inhibitor under supervision gives a documented safe option. Aspirin desensitization is available for those who need antiplatelet therapy or have aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
test.x: Skin testing and specific IgE are worthless here and are frequently ordered anyway - the reaction is not IgE-mediated. Challenge only where resuscitation is immediately available and never in uncontrolled asthma.

test.l: CRP, ESR, serum amyloid A, serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation
test.w: Recurrent wheals with fever, bone or joint pain, or an eruption that has resisted antihistamines for months with systemic symptoms.
test.p: Inflammatory markers raised between attacks push this out of ordinary urticaria entirely. A monoclonal IgM in an adult over 40 makes Schnitzler syndrome the leading diagnosis. Refer for interleukin-1 blockade and NLRP3 sequencing.
test.n: Normal markers between attacks argue strongly against an autoinflammatory syndrome and back toward chronic spontaneous urticaria.
test.x: Serum amyloid A is the marker that predicts the complication that actually kills - renal AA amyloidosis. Order it alongside CRP rather than instead of it.

test.l: Perilesional direct immunofluorescence and BP180 ELISA in pregnancy, read as negative for linear C3
test.w: Any urticarial eruption in pregnancy that starts periumbilically, blisters, began before the third trimester, or recurred earlier in a subsequent pregnancy.
test.p: Negative immunofluorescence in a third-trimester eruption that began in the striae and spares the umbilicus confirms polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, which needs only symptom control and reassurance.
test.n: Linear C3 with or without IgG at the basement membrane means this is pemphigoid gestationis, not polymorphic eruption of pregnancy. That changes everything: obstetric referral, fetal surveillance for prematurity and growth restriction, and systemic prednisone.
test.x: The two conditions are treated as interchangeable far too often. Periumbilical involvement and any blister are the features that should trigger the biopsy rather than another tube of emollient.

test.l: Environmental eradication trial with barrier measures
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §28; accuracy figures are a calibrated estimate
test.w: Recurrent crops of itchy papules with a central punctum on exposed skin, especially in children, travelers and pet owners.
test.p: No new lesions after treating pets, laundering and heat-treating bedding, and using repellent confirms the diagnosis and ends the search for an internal cause. Old lesions fade slowly and their persistence is not treatment failure.
test.n: Continued new crops after thorough eradication should redirect toward scabies, dermatitis herpetiformis, or papular pruritic eruption of HIV.
test.x: Families reject the diagnosis because only one member is affected. Explain that sensitization differs between people, or the eradication never gets done and the child is treated with steroids for months.

flag: If a wheal outlasts 24 hours, biopsy it. If swelling occurs without wheals and does not respond to adrenaline, it is bradykinin-mediated and needs a different drug entirely. These two rules resolve most of the diagnostic difficulty in this presentation.
